summary_plain: The SPICE investigation burned gaseous fuels such as methane, ethylene, propane, and propylene inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox aboard the International Space Station. By studying these flames in weightlessness, researchers can observe how non-buoyant diffusion flames behave without gravity-driven flow distortions. This research helps us understand soot formation and improves fire safety models for spacecraft.
summary_expert: SPICE (Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment) conducted tests using the MSG flow duct hardware on the International Space Station, running 435 tests in its experimental table and a total of 526 flames studied. The tested fuels and sample materials included methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, and mixtures of 50% and 75% propylene by volume in nitrogen. Burner jet nozzle geometries and sample diameters were 0.4064 mm (or 0.41 mm), 0.762 mm (or 0.76 mm), and 1.6002 mm (or 1.6 mm), with forced air flow speeds (co-flow velocities) ranging from 0.28 to 85.28 cm/s (or specifically 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s). Variables that were changed between tests included flow rate, fuel type, and burner geometry. Outcomes and measurements included determining laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames, luminous flame lengths, radiative heat losses, and co-flow air velocity distributions.

key_findings.text: Increasing coflow velocity decreases luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths.
Smaller burners have longer smoke points for coflowing flames.
The luminous flame lengths generally correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they increase slightly as air velocity decreases.

During Increment 18 SPICE conducted 108 test points completing its nominal test matrix, and during Increments 19/20 conducted 155 additional test points providing improved resolution of the smoke points.

earth_applications: refining computational models for predicting flame behaviors
better fuel formulations and combustion processes
